### Problem: Submarine in the Rybinsk Sea (hard edition) {#sec-nd-p4-rybinsk}

::: {.p-statement}
An array of $n$ integers $a_1,\dots,a_n$ in decimal with no leading zeros ($1 \le n \le 10^{5}$, $1 \le a_i \le 10^{9}$, and the numbers may have **different** lengths). $f(x, y)$ interleaves the digits of $x$ and $y$ **from the lowest digit up, taking $y$'s digit first**; when one number runs out, the other's remaining digits are written out as-is; the result is also assembled low-to-high. Examples: $f(1111,2222)=12121212$, $f(7777,888)=7787878$, $f(33,44444)=4443434$, $f(555,6)=5556$. Compute $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} f(a_i, a_j) \bmod 998244353$.

Source: [CF 1195D2 · Submarine in the Rybinsk Sea (hard edition)](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1195/D2){.solved rating="1800"}

Example — for $[12]$ the single pair is $f(12,12)=1122$; for $[5,6]$ the four pairs give $f(5,5){+}f(5,6){+}f(6,5){+}f(6,6)=55+56+65+66=242$; for $[11,12,13]$ the nine ordered pairs total `10098`. (Each checked against a replay of the definition, then stressed.)
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The double sum is over $n^2$ pairs — too many to build each $f$ for ($n \le 10^{5}$). So switch to **contribution**: ask, for each digit of each number, the place value ($10^{\text{power}}$) it lands on, summed over all its partners. That power depends only on the two numbers' **lengths** and the digit's position from the right, not on the digits themselves. In the alternating part a low digit of $y$ (first argument's partner) sits at $10^{2k}$ and a low digit of $x$ at $10^{2k+1}$; once the shorter number is exhausted the longer one's leftover digits march up consecutive powers. Group the input by length, precompute per-length digit sums, and the whole answer is a weighted sum over the $\le 10 \times 10$ length pairs — exactly the weighted-prefix / multiplicity idea of @sec-nd-a6, with the weight being a power of ten.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Build every pair.** For each ordered $(i,j)$ form $f(a_i,a_j)$ by interleaving and add. $O(n^2 \cdot \text{digits})$ — reference only.
2. **Digit contribution by length pair.** For lengths $p=\lvert x\rvert$, $q=\lvert y\rvert$: $x$'s $k$-th low digit (from the right, $k=0..p-1$) lands on power $2k+1$ while $k<\min(p,q)$, else on $q+k$; $y$'s $k$-th low digit lands on $2k$ while $k<\min(p,q)$, else on $p+k$. Accumulate $\text{sumdigits}[p][k]$ over all numbers of length $p$; a length pair $(p,q)$ contributes $\big(\sum_k \text{sumdigits}[p][k]\cdot10^{\text{xpow}}\big)\cdot \text{cnt}[q] + \big(\sum_k \text{sumdigits}[q][k]\cdot10^{\text{ypow}}\big)\cdot \text{cnt}[p]$.

**Invariant.** Every ordered pair is counted once by the term for its $(\lvert x\rvert, \lvert y\rvert)$, and each of its digits is charged the exact power the definition assigns it, so the weighted sum equals $\sum_{i,j} f(a_i,a_j)$.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Interleave every ordered pair

::: {.form-next}
Form $f(a_i, a_j)$ literally for all $n^2$ pairs and add. The oracle the fast form is checked against; $O(n^2)$ is reference only.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def ryb_interleave(x, y):
    """f(x, y): take digits from the right, y's first, alternating; a side that runs
    out stops contributing and the other continues; assemble the result low-to-high."""
    sx, sy = str(x), str(y)
    i = len(sx) - 1; j = len(sy) - 1
    out = []; turn = 0
    while i >= 0 or j >= 0:
        if turn == 0:
            if j >= 0:
                out.append(sy[j]); j -= 1
        else:
            if i >= 0:
                out.append(sx[i]); i -= 1
        turn ^= 1
    return int("".join(reversed(out)))


def ryb_brute(arr):
    s = 0
    for x in arr:
        for y in arr:
            s += ryb_interleave(x, y)
    return s % 998244353


assert ryb_interleave(1111, 2222) == 12121212
assert ryb_interleave(33, 44444) == 4443434
assert ryb_interleave(555, 6) == 5556
assert ryb_brute([5, 6]) == 242
```

##### C++

```cpp
// brute force: build f(x, y) for every ordered pair and add (fragment, needs <bits/stdc++.h>)
long long ryb_inter(long long x, long long y) {
    string sx = to_string(x), sy = to_string(y);
    int i = (int)sx.size() - 1, j = (int)sy.size() - 1, turn = 0;
    string out;
    while (i >= 0 || j >= 0) {
        if (turn == 0) { if (j >= 0) { out += sy[j]; j--; } }
        else           { if (i >= 0) { out += sx[i]; i--; } }
        turn ^= 1;
    }
    reverse(out.begin(), out.end());
    return stoll(out);
}
long long ryb_brute(const vector<long long>& a) {
    const long long MOD = 998244353;
    long long s = 0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < a.size(); ++i)
        for (size_t j = 0; j < a.size(); ++j)
            s = (s + ryb_inter(a[i], a[j])) % MOD;
    return s;
}
```
:::

#### Charge each digit its place value, grouped by length

::: {.form-next}
Group numbers by length, store per-length digit sums, and for each of the $\le 100$ length pairs add the weighted digit contributions. $O(n \cdot 10 + 100 \cdot 10)$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: sec-nd-p4-rybinsk-sol
def ryb_fish(arr):
    """Weighted digit-contribution over all ordered pairs, mod 998244353."""
    MOD = 998244353
    MAXL = 10
    cnt = [0] * (MAXL + 1)
    S = [[0] * (MAXL + 1) for _ in range(MAXL + 1)]   # S[p][k] = sum of k-th low digit
    for v in arr:
        d = str(v); plen = len(d); cnt[plen] += 1
        for k in range(plen):
            S[plen][k] += int(d[plen - 1 - k])
    pw10 = [1] * (2 * MAXL + 3)
    for i in range(1, len(pw10)):
        pw10[i] = pw10[i - 1] * 10 % MOD

    def xpow(p, q, k): return 2 * k + 1 if k < min(p, q) else q + k
    def ypow(p, q, k): return 2 * k     if k < min(p, q) else p + k

    ans = 0
    for p in range(1, MAXL + 1):
        if not cnt[p]:
            continue
        for q in range(1, MAXL + 1):
            if not cnt[q]:
                continue
            xpart = sum(S[p][k] * pw10[xpow(p, q, k)] for k in range(p)) % MOD * cnt[q] % MOD
            ypart = sum(S[q][k] * pw10[ypow(p, q, k)] for k in range(q)) % MOD * cnt[p] % MOD
            ans = (ans + xpart + ypart) % MOD
    return ans


assert ryb_fish([12]) == 1122
assert ryb_fish([5, 6]) == 242
assert ryb_fish([11, 12, 13]) == 10098
for _ in range(200):
    arr = [random.randint(1, 9999) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 7))]
    assert ryb_fish(arr) == ryb_brute(arr)
```

##### C++

```cpp
// weighted digit-contribution over all ordered pairs, full program (reads stdin)
const long long MOD = 998244353;
long long pw10r[25];
int rxbx(int p, int q, int k) { return k < min(p, q) ? 2 * k + 1 : q + k; }
int rxby(int p, int q, int k) { return k < min(p, q) ? 2 * k     : p + k; }
int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    int n;
    if (!(cin >> n)) return 0;
    const int MAXL = 10;
    vector<long long> cnt(MAXL + 1, 0);
    vector<vector<long long> > S(MAXL + 1, vector<long long>(MAXL + 1, 0));
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        long long v;
        cin >> v;
        string d = to_string(v);
        int p = (int)d.size();
        cnt[p]++;
        for (int k = 0; k < p; ++k) S[p][k] += d[p - 1 - k] - '0';
    }
    pw10r[0] = 1;
    for (int i = 1; i < 25; ++i) pw10r[i] = pw10r[i - 1] * 10 % MOD;
    long long ans = 0;
    for (int p = 1; p <= MAXL; ++p) if (cnt[p])
        for (int q = 1; q <= MAXL; ++q) if (cnt[q]) {
            long long xpart = 0;
            for (int k = 0; k < p; ++k) xpart = (xpart + (S[p][k] % MOD) * pw10r[rxbx(p, q, k)]) % MOD;
            xpart = xpart % MOD * cnt[q] % MOD;
            long long ypart = 0;
            for (int k = 0; k < q; ++k) ypart = (ypart + (S[q][k] % MOD) * pw10r[rxby(p, q, k)]) % MOD;
            ypart = ypart % MOD * cnt[p] % MOD;
            ans = (ans + xpart + ypart) % MOD;
        }
    cout << ans << "\n";
    return 0;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `d[plen-1-k]` is the $k$-th digit from the right, so `S[p][k]` totals that digit over every length-$p$ number. `xpow`/`ypow` are the two power formulas from the intuition: the alternating part ($2k$/$2k+1$) while both numbers still have digits, then the leftover of the longer one marching up from $q+k$ or $p+k$. Multiplying $x$'s total by `cnt[q]` accounts for every partner of length $q$ at once — that single factor is what collapses $O(n^2)$ pairs into $O(1)$ per length pair.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Build-every-pair:** $O(n^2 \cdot D)$ — reference only. **Digit contribution:** grouping is $O(nD)$ with $D \le 10$ digits; the double loop over length pairs is a constant $10 \times 10 \times 10$, so $O(nD + D^3)$ total. Space $O(D^2)$.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Equal lengths: the hard edition allows different lengths, which is exactly what the $2k+1$ / $2k$ "alternating part" plus the $q+k$ / $p+k$ "leftover" split handles; forgetting the leftover branch reproduces the (easier) same-length case only.
- $x$ shorter than $y$ and vice versa: `xpow` uses $q+k$ (valid only when $p>q$), `ypow` uses $p+k$ (only when $q>p$) — swap them and the longer number's digits land on wrong powers.
- Modulo $998244353$: reduce `pw10`, each digit term, and the pair counts — the raw weighted sum over $10^{10}$ pairs far exceeds 64-bit.
- $a_i$ up to $10^9$: $10$ digits, so `MAXL = 10` and the power index tops out at $q+k \le 19$, inside `pw10`.
:::
